narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the predictive model determined you had a 61% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt—meaning your risk of failure was greater than your chance of passing. This risk assessment is based on several academic indicators, and the three most influential factors, in order of impact, tell a clear story.

The strongest signal was your class standing in your third year. You were in the third decile, meaning a significant portion of your classmates ranked above you, and this placed you well below the average class standing of accepted students. This factor pushed the model strongly toward a prediction of failure. Your LSAT score also worked against you. At 33, it fell below the average of 37 for admitted applicants, further increasing the predicted likelihood of bar exam failure.

However, not everything pointed in a negative direction. Your undergraduate GPA was a point in your favor. At 3.90, it was considerably higher than the 3.23 average among accepted students, and this strong past performance pushed the model toward a passing prediction. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not enough to overcome the stronger negative signals from your third-year class rank and LSAT score.

What should you do next? Retake the LSAT to bring your score closer to or above the average of accepted students. Also, consider strengthening your final-year coursework to boost your class standing. Together, these improvements would demonstrate higher bar exam readiness and substantially improve your chances upon reapplication.
